sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
We have no continuous history for Karlsruhe: our data covers the Covid period to mid-2022 and then resumes in August 2026, so we show no trend. The garages we then measured fell from 29% occupied in April 2020 to about 26% in the winter of 2020/21. The occupancy figures below are for weekdays and weekends in August and September 2026.

Karlsruhe has chosen to reprice its streets rather than close them. After a fee rise in 2021 [0], the council set residents' permits at €180 a year for 2022 and 2023, up from €30, but rejected a step to €360 from 2024 [2]. In December 2025 it settled on raising on-street fees by 50% instead of doubling them, linked to a planned extension of the paid zones and of resident parking [11]. It adopted the amendment in March 2026, by 34 votes to 8 [12]. The ordinance sets €1.50 per 15 minutes in the central zone, €6 an hour, from 1 June 2026 [13]. The mayor made clear the increase concerns public street space only, not the garages, which the city mostly cannot influence [11]. The Kombilösung tram tunnel under Kaiserstraße opened in December 2021, with the road tunnel due to follow in March 2022 [1]. The city said in 2025 that it had no complete data on public parking yet, and planned a first coarse analysis as part of a parking concept [9].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The centre has been changing at its edges. The Peek & Cloppenburg building on Kaiserstraße and its car park were to be demolished for a new building [4], while the Galeria department store in the listed building opposite was kept open in 2023 [5]. In August 2026 two vehicles burned in Parkhaus Stephansplatz and about 60 others were towed out sooty; as of the next day it was not known when the garage would reopen [16]. Our figure for it may therefore not reflect normal use.

The city runs a guidance system: 21 garages with 8,105 spaces report free spaces to street signs and a mobility portal [8]. In 2021 the city's own garages offered only AC charging: seven points at Kronenplatz, two at the ZKM and two at the main station [3]. In August 2024 the city counted about 430 publicly accessible points, mostly at customer car parks, garages and petrol stations [6]. Saturday pedestrian counts at 20 points in the centre reached about 340,000 in spring 2025, against 195,500 in spring 2020, under Covid rules [14]. Visitors still rate the centre's attractiveness at 2.8 on a school-grade scale where lower is better, worse than 2.6 in 2022 [15].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Karlsruhe's centre is compact: every garage we measure lies within a kilometre of the Marktplatz, and the 14 together average 31% on weekdays and 27% at weekends, so the centre draws visitors all week. PBW (Parkraumgesellschaft Baden-Württemberg) runs the largest, Schlossplatz (912 spaces, €2 an hour, €10 a day), at 46% on weekdays and 30% at weekends. The Ettlinger Tor centre's garage, with 843 spaces, stands at 20%. The cheapest garage we hold prices for, Kronenplatz, at €1 an hour and €7.50 a day, is at 28%. The street at €6 an hour is about three times as dear as the €2 garages.

Occupancy follows destinations more than price. The small garage behind the C&A store on Kreuzstraße is the fullest (77%, 85% at weekends), followed by the Karstadt (54%) and Stephansplatz (54%) garages. The city says the main-station garage is the one with especially high use and that its prices are agreed with Deutsche Bahn [10]. We do not yet measure it. The emptiest are Luisenstraße (6%) and the second Congress Centre garage (10%).
